content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
This paper presents a method for adaptively selecting the positive samples in triplet loss. Based on the assumption that the norm of the gradient of the loss correlates with the informativeness of each sample, the authors theoretically motivate and propose a method to adaptively select the positive examples. On an evaluation on two datasets, the authors show some mild improvements over the HardNet baseline.

Overall, the suggested method seems reasonable, but the evaluation seems weak.

* The reported results are far from beating the baseline with a "significant margin" as the authors claim.

* It's unclear if the results are reported over multiple runs or a single run. Since this isn't reported, a single run is insufficient to suggest how this method actually works. For example, what is the variance among different trainings?

* Arguably, the demonstration of this method in two datasets is somewhat weak too. Adding more datasets can strengthen this work.

* The authors argue in Appendix E that AdaSample converges faster. However, this is computed in terms of number of epochs not computation time. How does this method compare in terms of computation time? AdaSample adds some additional computational complexity over HardNet.

* One could imagine that the negative samples of the triplet loss can also be sampled in a similar way. Instead the authors opt for the "hardest-in-batch" negatives. Why is such a decision made? Does AdaSample _not_ work for negative samples?

Overall, I find this work interesting and I would like to see it eventually published. However, at this moment, it is unclear to me (and to any reader, I assume) if the additional complexity introduced by this method actually yields performance improvements.

content.title: Replies
content.comment:
1. More Datasets:
We agree that adding more datasets can better demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. However, UBC PhotoTour and HPatches are the most widely-used datasets, and are sufficient to demonstrate our contribution. Besides, we conduct experiments on ETH SfM dataset, whose results are shown in the Appendix D.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper proposes a novel patch sampling method to construct effective mini-batch for training networks based on a triplet loss.
In the proposed method, matching pairs of patches are drawn as positive samples stochastically according to the “informativeness” which is defined by means of the derivatives of loss.
The authors provide theoretical justification for the novel criterion as well as the practically useful formulation only dependent on the descriptor distance.
The experimental results on the patch matching tasks using several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in comparison with the other learning-based descriptors.

The proposed sampling criterion contributes to effectively training the patch descriptors and I like the simple method that is well founded on the theoretical backgrounds.
Though, there are some ambiguous points to be clarified by the authors.

* The concept of “class” is unclear. How is it defined in this framework? Generally speaking, a local patch is not necessarily connected to the object classes but rather related to the lower-level image structures, such as edges and curvatures. Thus, it seems to be difficult to assign/define specific class labels for patches in the framework of learning patch descriptor in contrast to object classification. And, through the theoretical derivation for the method, the class categories seem not to be necessary. Clarify what kind (level) of class is assumed to establish the proposed sampling method. 

* The hyper parameter \lambda in Eq.(13) might be difficult to tune since we don’t have prior knowledge about the loss value. Is it possible to robustly set \lambda by certain value, say 10, across various datasets and networks?; in the experiment, \lambda=10 exhibits favorable performance. And, it would be better to show the values of \alpha in Eq.(12) throughout the training by \lambda=10.

* In the experiment, is the angle loss Eq.(15) applied to the HardNet? For fair comparison, the network should be trained based on the same loss. In addition, the authors should show the performance results of lambda=0 to clarify the effectiveness of lambda>0.

* Fig.1 is poorly presented in terms both of the coloring (markers) and image quality; it is hard to see even on the screen.

* Show the comparison regarding training time. Although the method contributes to faster convergence, it requires extra computational cost in computing the descriptor distances via forward-pass of the network.

content.title: Replies
content.comment:
1. Concept of "Class":
The term ``class'' in this paper stands for the image patches extracted from the same 3D location. We agree with your concerns, and we will clarify this concept in next version.
2. Hyper-parameter $\lambda$:
From our heuristics, a hard task requires a relatively large $\lambda$, and verse vica. For example, $\lambda=2$ works best for image matching, while $\lambda=10$ works best for patch verification and patch retrieval (Tab. 2). A potential explanation is that for a tough task, normal patches cannot be easily discriminated, so imposing a large $\lambda$ may result in normal examples not sufficiently trained. However, in our experiments, setting $\lambda=10$ can give satisfactory results on both UBC PhotoTour and HPatches datasets.
3. Comparison with HardNet: For comparison with HardNet, we adopt the official pretrained model provided by its authors, in which Euclidean distance is used. Besides, the ablation studies towards different distance metrics, as shown in Tab. 2, are sufficient to verify the superority of the angular distance on top of Euclidean distance. For $\lambda = 0$, AdaSample degrades into HardNet baseline, so Fig. 1 demonstrates the performance of HardNet (i.e., $\lambda=0$) when trained on either Liberty or HPatches dataset.
4. Quality of Fig. 1: Thanks for your suggestion. We will improve that in next version.

content.title: This paper proposes a novel method on triplet mining, which adaptively selects hard similar examples to minimizing the expected parameter rectification.
content.comment:
Pro:
1.	The idea of this paper is well motivated and the theoretical contribution as stated in Theorem 1 and 2 is interesting.

Cons:
1.	The authors argue that selecting the most dissimilar matching pairs may induce the network with bias in favor if dissimilar matching pairs. Similarly, it is natural to think that select the most similar non-matching pairs may also induce training bias. However, this paper only focuses the former problem. Is this paper still suffers from the latter problem? More theoretical analysis is needed to support the statement. 
2.	There is a constrain that the gradient estimator G_{i} is an unbiased estimator of the gradient. Please elaborate why this constrain is needed and the corresponding benefits. 
3.	The authors prove that maximizing R_{t} is equivalent to minimizing tr(Var[G_{I_{t}}]) based on pointwise loss function, however, the matching distance approximation is derived with triplet loss function. Please give detail explanation about this discrepancy.

replying_to: Replying to This paper proposes a novel method on triplet mining, which adaptively selects hard similar examples to minimizing the expected parameter rectification.

content.title: Replies
content.comment:
1. Necessity of Unbiasedness:
The unbiasedness is a necessary assumption for optimization with SGD because it can facilitate optimization and guarantee convergence under mild conditions. The non-asymptotic error bound of unbiased gradient estimates is referred to [1*]. For re-weighted SGD, as in our case, the improved convergence rate can be found in [2*]. Also, unbiasedness is widely assumed in \textit{importance sampling} literature [2*,3*]. Our adaptive sampling method also falls into the re-weighted SGD category (see Equ. 3, 13). Therefore, we share the same spirits with prior works [2*,3*], and adopt unbiasedness as a basic assumption of our derivation.
2. Discrepancy between pointwise loss and triplet loss:
We derive our formulation in Thm. 1 based on pointwise loss because of its simplicity and generality. If we view each anchor-positive-negative triplet as an identity to be sampled, then the triplet loss becomes pointwise loss. Employing the same reasoning as in Sec. 3.2, we can reach the same formulation in Eqn. 11, which is generic and independent of the specific form of the loss function. Then, with the specific form of triplet loss, we give approximations of $\mathcal{L}$ and $\nabla \mathcal{L}$, and reach our final sampling formulation in Eqn. 13.

[1*] http://papers.nips.cc/paper/4316-non-asymptotic-analysis-of-stochastic-approximation-algorithms-for-machine-learning (NIPS'11);
[2*] https://papers.nips.cc/paper/5355-stochastic-gradient-descent-weighted-sampling-and-the-randomized-kaczmarz-algorithm (NIPS'14);
[3*] https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.00942 (ICML'18).

content.title: Official Blind Review #4
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
The paper proposes to make two modifications in hard negative mining procedure for descriptor learning:
 - instead of selecting hardest samples in a minibatch it proposes to sample proportionally to distance between descriptors
 - gradient wrt model parameters is weighted inverse proportionally to the distance
The authors attempt to analyze the method theoretically and evaluate on two descriptor learning benchmarks, UBC phototour 2011 and HPatches 2017.

I propose reject mainly for the following reasons:
1) dataset selection and quality of experimental evaluation
2) the writing (presentation of the results)

Regarding (1), my main concern is on statistical significance of presented experiments. The authors conduct each experiment once and do not take into account variance coming from neural net training. For example, in table 2 all numbers seem to be very close so it is not possible to conclude anything. Same is true for other experiments, one way to improve would be to do 10-fold cross validation or at least train 5 network with different random seed and provide mean +- std of the results.

Then, I think UBC results are not indicative of performance since the dataset is small and very old at this point, so I disagree with the claim that improvement of ~0.1% is of significant margin. Improvement on HPatches seems to be slightly more significant, but it is not clear wether the authors used comparable networks in terms of number of parameters in the network and descriptor size.

Regarding (2), the way the paper is written is very confusing and should be improved. The attempts to have a theoretical derivation of the proposed method are welcome, but should not precede the actual explanation of the method. I suggest to explain clearly the modifications to sampling strategy, and only then relate them to informativeness intuition.

Further, the improvement over HardNet is not clear. The two proposed modifications are not tested separately. To have a proper ablation study, the authors could sample negatives proportionally to descriptor distance and remove gradient weighting, and vice versa, to sample hardest-in-batch and only add gradient weighting.

I also disagree that hard negative mining is "widely used in object detection and other vision tasks" (quoting the authors). It used to be common in metric learning for face recognition, as the authors cite FaceNet 2015, but has been long abandoned in favor of SphereFace-like approaches. Same is true for object detection, where Fast R-CNN and Mask R-CNN without HNM are widely used.

content.title: Replies
content.comment:
1. Performance Gain:
We argue that our performance gain is still significant as our baseline, i.e., HardNet, is strong. For example, consider 1.15% v.s. 1.05% in Tab. 1. The absolute improvement of 0.1% seems not significant, while the relative improvement of 8.7% is indeed ``"a significant margin". Besides, We use the same model with L2-Net and HardNet, without bringing any extra parameters.
2. Organization of the Paper:
We derive our sampling method step by step based on the optimization mechanism of SGD, and finally reach our sampling formulation (Eqn. 13). We organize our paper in this way so as to avoid the abrupt occurrence of our method for no theoretical reasoning. Still, we will carefully consider your suggestion, and briefly introduce our algorithm in the beginning.
3. Separate Ablations:
We argue that our sampling probabilities and re-weighting scalars are derived simultaneously in our paper. So only incorporating a single component will undermine the theoretical guarantees. Besides, in our primary experiments, we found that we can still achieve comparable performance without the re-weighting scalars. However, for the theoretical completeness, we include them in our algorithm. Potentially, the re-weighting scalars can lead to better performance on future datasets due to the theoretical guarantees.
4. Popularity of Hard Negative Mining:
Hard negative mining is still an active research field in machine learning and computer vision community. Refer to the following recent papers [1*,2*,3*] that focus on hard negative mining.

[1*] https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.05503v1 (CVPR'19);
[2*] http://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_CVPR_2019/papers/Suh_Stochastic_Class-Based_Hard_Example_Mining_for_Deep_Metric_Learning_CVPR_2019_paper.pdf (CVPR'19);
[3*] http://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_ICCV_2019/papers/Sun_MVP_Matching_A_Maximum-Value_Perfect_Matching_for_Mining_Hard_Samples_ICCV_2019_paper.pdf (ICCV'2019).

content.title: Unified Reply to Common Concerns
content.comment:
1. Hard Negatives (To Deng & R3): 
    The positives are selected from the whole dataset, and selecting the hardest one may introduce a bias. However, the negatives are selected within a mini-batch, where the hardest negative in a batch is not the hardest one in the dataset. So the bias has been compensated by the batch size. Besides, the efficacy of hardest-in-batch solution has been demonstrated in HardNet, so we share the same spirits with HardNet, and contribute by selecting the hard positives.
2. Convergence Speed in terms of Training Time (To R1 & R3): 
    Although the sampling brings extra computational cost, our trained model enjoy equal computational complexity and time consumption with HardNet baseline in inference.
3. Statistical Significance of Performance Improvement and Repeated Experiments (To R3 & R4):
    We believe that the performance improvement is significant, especially in non-saturated tasks, e.g., image matching and patch retrieval results in Fig. 1. 
    For repeated experiments, as far as we know, no prior knowledge in descriptor learning gives such suggestion. Still, we conduct 5 individual experiments with different random seeds, and find that the performance variation is very minor. For example, on UBC PhotoTour dataset, the patch classification results are 1.254$\pm$0.026, 2.212$\pm$0.049, 0.400$\pm$0.016, 0.627$\pm$0.012, 1.395$\pm$0.050, 1.137$\pm$0.036, respectively. As a result, we can conclude that our sampling solution is stable against various random conditions.
    Also, we performed the classic Mann-Whitney testing for the statistical significance of our improvement. Results demonstrate that our improvement is statistically significant in most of the experimental settings. Therefore, we can conclude that our improvement does not result from stochasticity.
